interest: This document is valuable to historians studying American intelligence monitoring, counterespionage, and surveillance of expatriates in the South Pacific leading up to and during World War II. It highlights the case of Henry Walsworth Kinney, a well-known American journalist and longtime publicist for the South Manchuria Railway, illustrating how Westerners with past Japanese affiliations were tracked across remote territories like French Oceania. Additionally, the docket captures the fluidity of wartime counterintelligence suspicions, showing how allegations against Kinney in Tahiti transitioned from gathering intelligence for Tokyo in 1938 to suspected Nazi espionage with his wife by mid-1942.
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.20251M, File 47) consists of a 'List of Papers' docket sheet for a non-jacket case concerning Japanese military and espionage activities in the Society Islands (French Oceania) between 1938 and 1942. The documented correspondence focuses on Henry Walsworth Kinney, an American citizen and former publicist for the South Manchuria Railway residing in Tahiti, who was suspected of acting as an espionage agent for the Japanese government and supplying reports on French Oceania. The docket records reports from U.S. consular officers in Tahiti (Scudder Mersman and Lambert), liaison with J. Edgar Hoover at the Department of Justice, transmissions to the U.S. embassy in Japan, and a 1942 report noting that Kinney and his wife were suspected of being Nazi agents living in the district of Mataiea.

subfiles.about: A State Department 'List of Papers' docket sheet recording five communications between 1938 and 1942 regarding suspected Japanese and Nazi espionage activities of Henry Walsworth Kinney in Tahiti.
subfiles.summary: This docket sheet catalogs five documents under decimal file 894.20251M relating to Japanese military and espionage activities in the Society Islands from March 1938 to June 1942. It details reports from U.S. consular representatives in Tahiti, Scudder Mersman and Lambert, regarding allegations that American citizen Henry Walsworth Kinney was reporting on French Oceania for the Japanese government and later suspected, along with his wife, of being Nazi agents residing in Mataiea. The sheet also tracks cross-departmental communication with J. Edgar Hoover of the Department of Justice, transmissions to the diplomatic post in Japan, and cross-references to Charles Bishop Kinney.
subfiles.title: List of Papers: Japanese military and espionage activities in Society Islands
